Q: Why did yandaredevs code suck A:

Get some good books and start reading. You can't learn to program from scattered videos online until you know enough of the language to be able to filter out frauds and the helpful folk who legitimately think they're much better programmers than they are. Frankly you can't learn to do much from online videos alone. Anyone can post anything online, and most of them are going to be wrong. Plus there are far too many content farmers who don't care if you got anything useful from the video so long as they got the views and ad money that comes with it.

On the internet your best bet is to find out who the experts in the subject you're interested in are and use the resources they provide or recommend.

Here's a list of good books on C++. Someone else will have to help out with Python links.

If you can't afford books after slapping down cash for a new computer, and I can't blame you with today's prices, LearnCpp.com is surprisingly good for free.

The CPPCon videos are generally good, though most will be delving deeper than beginner material.

The rest is practice. Depending on how far you want to go, that can be years and years of practice.

And now to be the dreaded Stack Overflow Elitist: Read the instructions on how to use the site, particularly the section on asking questions, before you accidentally get yourself banned. Things are a looser with Advice-type questions, but the same general formula applies. Get to the point quickly, avoid rants, provide good examples, and keep the focus of the question as narrow as possible.

The primary goal of Stack Overflow is to build a library of high-quality answers to questions that can be used by present and future programmers. If you ask a question that's only usable by you, it's not going to be a useful addition to the library. If future askers give up half-way through a question before you get to the point, it's not useful. If you ask too much all at once, it's not going to be very useful because the answers will sprawl.

As a beginner you'll find there's not a lot you can ask about in established languages like C++ and Python that hasn't already been asked, so search the library first.

Q: Do any ARMv8 processors exhibit load buffering? A:

I found the answer on this website: the Snapdragon 820 SoC and the Amlogic S922X SoC both exhibit LB. Every other machine of the two dozen machines they tested did not exhibit it.

Q: Producing messages from Clickhouse materialized view to Kafka topic by Kafka Engine writes messages with key=null A:

The issue comes from how ClickHouse maps the Kafka message key.

In the Kafka table engine, the special column `_key` must be of type String. If it's not, ClickHouse won't use it as the Kafka message key and it will default to null.

In your case:

toYYYYMMDD(source_day) as _key

returns a numeric value, not a string.

Fix it by converting it explicitly:

toString(toYYYYMMDD(source_day)) as _key

or simply:

toString(source_day) as _key

After that, Kafka will correctly use this field as the message key.

More generally, when working with ClickHouse + Kafka:

- Kafka engine acts like a stream consumer

- Materialized views act as transformation triggers

- Proper schema mapping (types!) is critical

If you're exploring real-time pipelines with ClickHouse and Kafka, understanding this mapping layer is key.

If you're learning how ClickHouse integrates with Kafka and how materialized views work in real-time pipelines, this explains it step by step:

https://idea2dev.com/en/learning/kafka-ai-real-time-data-pipelines-2026

Q: reading lines in from a text file and sorting them into a linked list java A:

Modern Java

We can use the features in modern Java to simplify this code.

Represent the location of the file with Path.of.

Get a Stream of String objects, one per line in file, by calling Files.lines. Use try-with-resources syntax to automatically close the stream, and its open file, in either case of successful or exceptional execution.

We count line numbers using AtomicInteger for its convenient getAndIncrement method.

Each line in the file is represented with our custom class Line. We store text of the line one field. In another field we store our calculated line number.

We call Stream#map to process the file’s lines. For each line, we instantiate a Line object. Those instances are then sorted with a Comparator, using two criteria.

First we sort by the length of the text of each line. Do not calculate the length by calling the legacy method String#length. That method is based on the char primitive type. The char type has been essentially broken since Java 2, and legacy since Java 5. As a 16-bit value, char is physically incapable of representing most characters. Learn to use Unicode code points to work with individual characters. Get a count of code points via the IntStream produced by String#codePoints.

Be aware that in some text, what appears to the human reader to be a single character may actually be composed of multiple code points, such as diacritical (accent marks) and emoji with natural skin tones. If this causes a problem for your situation, you’ll need to modify this code.

As our second sort criterion, we sort by the line number. This criterion applies to sort Line objects whose text has the same length.

We terminate our stream by producing a sorted List of Line objects. You may want to refer to this collection by its higher super-interface, SequencedCollection.

record Line(int lineNumber, String text) {}  // Define a class to halted each’s text and
SequencedCollection < String > linesSorted = null ;
Path path = Path.of( "path/to/example-txt" ) ;
try 
        (
                Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(path) 
        ) 
{
    AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger(1); // Count line numbers. 
    linesSorted = 
            lines
                    .map( text -> new Line( counter.getAndIncrement() , text ) )
                    .sorted(
                            Comparator
                                    .comparingInt( (Line l) -> l.text().codePoints().count() )
                                    .thenComparingInt( Line :: lineNumber ) 
                    )
                    .toList();
        }
`
